--- engine: knitr filters: - webr webr: show-startup-message: true cell-options: autorun: true --- # Project Control Systems ## Learning Objectives By the end of this chapter you will be able to: 1. **Describe** the monitoring-and-control loop and the performance measurement baseline. 2. **Read** the three earned-value curves: planned value (PV), earned value (EV), and actual cost (AC). 3. **Compute** schedule and cost variance and the SPI / CPI performance indices. 4. **Forecast** with EAC, ETC, VAC, and TCPI, and interpret them. 5. **Run** integrated change control so the baseline stays meaningful. 6. **Report** status honestly and recognize the "watermelon" trap.
Before we begin: the project has spent 60 % of its money --- is it 60 % done? Almost certainly not. "Percent of budget spent" and "percent of work finished" are different numbers, and the gap between them is the whole subject of this chapter.
## Introduction: from a plan to a control system You have planned the RC-vehicle project --- scope, WBS, schedule, budget. It is now **week 8**. The sponsor asks the only question that matters at this stage: **are we on track, and if not, how far off, and what will it cost to finish?** Answering that needs a **control system**: a closed loop that **measures** progress, **compares** it to the baseline, **analyzes** the variance, and drives a corrective **action** --- then measures again. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The monitoring-and-control loop. Without the 'compare to baseline' step, status reporting is just activity; with it, you get variance you can act on.](12-Project-Control-Systems_files/figure-html/fig-control-loop-12-1.png){#fig-control-loop-12 fig-align='center' width=864} ::: ::: The reference for "compare" is the **performance measurement baseline** --- the approved **scope + schedule + cost** locked in at the end of planning ([Chapter 9](09-Cost-Estimation-and-Budgeting.qmd)'s S-curve is its cost dimension). ::: {.callout-note} **Industry snapshot.** Earned value management is **contractually mandated** on large U.S. defense programs (EIA-748). Automotive programs run a lighter version at the milestone level. A food-plant capital project tracks committed vs. spent vs. installed. The math below is the same at every scale. :::
## The three curves Earned value management tracks three cumulative quantities against time: | Term | Also called | Meaning | |---|---|---| | **PV** --- Planned Value | BCWS | The budgeted cost of the work **scheduled** to be done by now | | **EV** --- Earned Value | BCWP | The budgeted cost of the work **actually done** by now | | **AC** --- Actual Cost | ACWP | What has actually been **spent** to do that work | **BAC** (Budget At Completion) is the total baseline budget --- where the PV curve ends. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The three curves through week 8 of the RC-vehicle project (BAC = $620 000, off the top of this view). By the status date EV sits below PV -- behind schedule -- and AC sits above EV -- over cost. The vertical gaps at week 8 are the schedule and cost variances.](12-Project-Control-Systems_files/figure-html/fig-evm-curves-12-1.png){#fig-evm-curves-12 fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## The six core metrics $$ \begin{aligned} \text{Schedule Variance} \quad SV &= EV - PV \\ \text{Cost Variance} \quad CV &= EV - AC \\ \text{Schedule Performance Index} \quad SPI &= EV / PV \\ \text{Cost Performance Index} \quad CPI &= EV / AC \end{aligned} $$ | Reading | Schedule | Cost | |---|---|---| | **Ahead / under** | $SV > 0$, $SPI > 1$ | $CV > 0$, $CPI > 1$ | | **On plan** | $SV = 0$, $SPI = 1$ | $CV = 0$, $CPI = 1$ | | **Behind / over** | $SV < 0$, $SPI < 1$ | $CV < 0$, $CPI < 1$ | ### Worked Example 1: the RC-vehicle project at week 8 Baseline budget **BAC = \$620 000**. By week 8 the plan said **35 %** of the work should be done; **30 %** is actually done; **\$210 000** has been spent. Live cell --- change the planned %, the actual %, or the actual cost. ```{=html}

Earned Value Calculator

Teaching demo
```
Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: evm-example-12 BAC <- 620000 planned_pct <- 0.35 actual_pct <- 0.30 AC <- 210000 PV <- planned_pct * BAC EV <- actual_pct * BAC SV <- EV - PV CV <- EV - AC SPI <- EV / PV CPI <- EV / AC money <- function(x) paste0(ifelse(x < 0, "-", ""), "$", format(round(abs(x)), big.mark = " ", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)) par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) bp <- barplot(c(PV, EV, AC) / 1000, names.arg = c("PV", "EV", "AC"), col = c("#bdc3c7", "#16a085", ifelse(AC > EV, "#e74c3c", "#2980b9")), ylim = c(0, 1100), ylab = "$ thousand", main = "Planned vs. earned vs. actual") sched <- if (SV < 0) "!!behind schedule!!" else "on or ahead of schedule" cost <- if (CV < 0) "!!over budget!!" else "on or under budget" cat(sprintf("Project is %s and %s\n", sched, cost)) cat(sprintf("Planned value (PV) %s\n", money(PV))) cat(sprintf("Earned value (EV) %s\n", money(EV))) cat(sprintf("Actual cost (AC) %s\n", money(AC))) cat(sprintf("Schedule variance (SV) %s\n", money(SV))) cat(sprintf("Cost variance (CV) %s\n", money(CV))) cat(sprintf("SPI %.3f (%.0f cents of schedule per planned dollar)\n", SPI, SPI * 100)) cat(sprintf("CPI %.3f (%.0f cents of work per dollar spent)\n", CPI, CPI * 100)) ```
The project is **behind schedule and over cost** --- and this is visible in week 8, while there is still time to act, instead of as a surprise at the end. ## PV, EV and AC are running totals from day 0 The three numbers in Worked Example 1 are not "this week's" numbers, and they are not the numbers for one task. Each one is a **running total for the whole project, from the first day up to the status date**: - **PV** adds up the budget of *all* the work the plan said would be done between week 0 and the status date --- including work packages that were planned to finish weeks ago. - **EV** adds up the budget value of *all* the work actually completed since week 0, finished packages included. - **AC** adds up *all* the money actually spent since week 0. A work package that finished in week 2 still counts in PV, EV and AC at week 8. That is why the curves in the figure above only ever go up. The project's **SPI** and **CPI** are then the ratios of those project totals: $SPI = \sum EV / \sum PV$ and $CPI = \sum EV / \sum AC$. You may work out the variance of each work package to find *where* the trouble is, but the project status always comes from the totals. ::: {.callout-warning} **Common mistake: averaging the task indices.** Never work out a CPI or SPI for each task and then average them. An average treats a \$4 000 decal job the same as a \$250 000 tooling package, and a task that has only just started (EV still 0) drags the average towards zero. The project CPI weights every task by its dollars automatically, because it divides the totals. ::: ::: {#tbl-evm-average-trap-12 .cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
Averaging task CPIs hides an overrun. The project CPI comes from the totals.
Package EV ($) AC ($) CPI
Tooling 2e+05 250 000 0.80
Labels and decals 6e+03 4 000 1.50
WRONG: average of the two CPIs 1.15 (looks under budget)
RIGHT: project totals 206 000 254 000 0.81 (over budget)
````` ::: ::: The average says the project earns \$1.15 of work for every dollar spent. In fact it earns only 0.81: about 19 cents of every dollar spent so far bought no work. ### Class exercise: PV, EV and AC from the time-phased plan This exercise builds the three numbers from scratch, the way a project control system does. A four-package project has a **time-phased budget**: the planned spend of each work package in each week (the S-curve data from [Chapter 9](09-Cost-Estimation-and-Budgeting.qmd)). The status date is the **end of week 6**. **What to do.** 1. In the first table, add across each row to get the **planned spend for that week**, then keep a **running total** from week 1. The running total at the status date is the project's **PV**. 2. In the second table, find each package's **PV to the end of week 6** (the sum of its planned spend in weeks 1 to 6) and check that the four add up to the PV from step 1. Then find each package's **EV = BAC x % complete**. The actual costs are given: they are everything booked to each package since week 1. 3. Add each column for the **project totals**, then compute the project SPI, CPI and EAC from those totals. **What it means.** Design finished in week 4, but its full budget still counts in PV, EV and AC at week 6: completed work never drops out of the totals. Assembly was planned to start in week 6 and has not started, so it adds to PV but nothing to EV --- that is part of why the project is behind. ```{=html}
``` ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution **Step 1.** The weekly planned spend is \$10 000, \$10 000, \$25 000, \$25 000, \$15 000, \$27 000, \$27 000, \$33 000, \$20 000 and \$8 000. The running total is \$10 000, \$20 000, \$45 000, \$70 000, \$85 000, **\$112 000**, \$139 000, \$172 000, \$192 000 and \$200 000 (the BAC). PV at the end of week 6 is **\$112 000**. **Step 2.** PV by package to the end of week 6: Design \$40 000 (all four of its weeks), Tooling \$60 000 (weeks 3 to 6), Assembly \$12 000 (week 6), Testing \$0. They add up to the same \$112 000. EV: Design 100 % of \$40 000 = \$40 000, Tooling 55 % of \$90 000 = \$49 500, Assembly and Testing \$0, so EV = **\$89 500**. AC = \$44 000 + \$58 000 = **\$102 000**. **Project status.** SPI = 89 500 / 112 000 = **0.799** (behind schedule), CPI = 89 500 / 102 000 = **0.877** (over cost), and EAC = 200 000 / 0.877 = **about \$227 900**. Assembly has not started on time: it carries \$12 000 of PV and no EV, and that is a schedule warning even though it has cost nothing yet.
### Try it yourself: earned value by work package Each work package has its budget, how much of it was planned to be done **by now, counting from the start of the project**, how much is actually done, and everything it has cost since the start. Design was planned to finish weeks ago, so its whole budget is in PV. Work out PV, EV, CV and SV for each package, add the columns to get the **project totals**, and only then compute the project SPI, CPI and forecast from those totals. Each team picks its own **data set**. ```{=html}
```
Show the worked solution PV = BAC x planned %, EV = BAC x actual %, CV = EV - AC, SV = EV - PV, all counted from the start of the project. For data set 1 the project totals are BAC \$620 000, PV **\$423 000**, EV **\$347 000** and AC **\$386 000**, so SPI = 347 / 423 = **0.820**, CPI = 347 / 386 = **0.899** and EAC = 620 000 / 0.899 = **about \$689 700**. Design finished long ago, yet its full \$120 000 is still in PV, EV and AC. Tooling is the package doing the damage: it is both behind (SV = -\$52 000) and over (CV = -\$23 000). Now try the wrong way. The four package CPIs are 0.952, 0.888, 0.865 and 0 (Testing has spent \$3 000 and earned nothing yet). Their average is 0.676, which says the project is losing a third of every dollar. It is not: weighted by the dollars, the true project CPI is 0.899. In data set 3 the trap runs the other way: the package CPIs average 1.05 ("under budget") while the project CPI is 0.996. Always divide the totals.
## Forecasting | Forecast | Formula | Meaning | |---|---|---| | **EAC** (Estimate At Completion) | $BAC / CPI$ | Total cost if current cost efficiency holds | | EAC (schedule too) | $AC + \dfrac{BAC - EV}{CPI \times SPI}$ | If both cost *and* schedule performance persist | | EAC (one-off overrun) | $AC + (BAC - EV)$ | If the overrun so far was a one-time event | | **ETC** (Estimate To Complete) | $EAC - AC$ | Money still needed from here | | **VAC** (Variance At Completion) | $BAC - EAC$ | Projected total over/under budget | | **TCPI** (To-Complete Performance Index) | $\dfrac{BAC - EV}{BAC - AC}$ | The cost efficiency the *remaining* work must hit to still land on BAC | ### Try it yourself: EAC scenarios ```{=html}

Estimate-at-Completion Scenarios

$

Challenge: Find the actual cost to date at which the original budget is still achievable (TCPI of 1 or less).
```
Show the live R code behind this calculator The card above re-runs this exact webR code every time you change an input, substituting your values for the variables at the top. Edit the code directly and press **Run Code** to experiment further. ```{webr-r} #| label: eac-scenarios-12 BAC <- 620000 EV <- 186000 AC <- 210000 PV <- 217000 CPI <- EV / AC SPI <- EV / PV eac_cpi <- BAC / CPI eac_oneoff <- AC + (BAC - EV) eac_cost_sched<- AC + (BAC - EV) / (CPI * SPI) etc <- eac_cpi - AC vac <- BAC - eac_cpi tcpi <- (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) money <- function(x) paste0(ifelse(x < 0, "-", ""), "$", format(round(abs(x)), big.mark = " ", scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE)) eacs <- c("BAC\n(plan)" = BAC, "CPI\ncontinues" = eac_cpi, "One-off\noverrun" = eac_oneoff, "Cost and\nschedule" = eac_cost_sched) par(mar = c(5, 5, 3, 1), cex.main = 1.3, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.1) barplot(eacs / 1000, col = c("#bdc3c7", "#2980b9", "#16a085", "#8e44ad"), ylim = c(0, max(eacs) / 1000 * 1.1), ylab = "$ thousand", main = "Estimate at completion by scenario") abline(h = BAC / 1000, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#e74c3c") msg <- if (tcpi > 1.10) { "!!a big ask; the BAC is likely unrealistic now!!" } else if (tcpi > 1.0) { "recoverable, but the team must run leaner than planned" } else { "achievable" } cat(sprintf("TCPI %.3f: %s\n", tcpi, msg)) cat(sprintf("CPI %.3f\n", CPI)) cat(sprintf("SPI %.3f\n", SPI)) cat(sprintf("EAC, cost efficiency continues %s\n", money(eac_cpi))) cat(sprintf("EAC, overrun was a one-off %s\n", money(eac_oneoff))) cat(sprintf("EAC, cost AND schedule persist %s\n", money(eac_cost_sched))) cat(sprintf("ETC (money still needed) %s\n", money(etc))) cat(sprintf("VAC (projected overrun) %s\n", money(vac))) ```
Which EAC formula should you actually report? It depends on *why* you are over. If a one-time event caused it (a failed test you have since fixed), $AC + (BAC - EV)$ is fair. If the overrun reflects how the team is fundamentally working (rates, productivity), $BAC/CPI$ is the honest number. If you are *also* behind schedule and recovery will cost overtime, the $CPI \times SPI$ version is the most conservative. Report the one your evidence supports --- and say which assumption you made.
### Try it yourself: which forecast do you report? ```{=html}
``` ## Reading the S-curve honestly - **Spend is not progress.** A project can be on budget (AC ≈ PV) and badly behind (EV ≪ PV) --- it just has not done the work yet. - **The "watermelon" report** --- green on the outside, red on the inside. High-level status shows green because spend matches plan, while the earned value underneath is red. - **Leading vs. lagging indicators.** SPI and CPI are somewhat lagging. Leading signals --- rising defect find-rate, slipping sub-milestones, key staff leaving --- warn you earlier. Watch both. ### Try it yourself: read the status ```{=html}
``` ## Integrated change control Control only works against a **meaningful baseline**. Every change request goes through the same gate as in [Chapter 3](03-Scope-and-Organizational-Structures.qmd): assess the impact on scope, schedule, and cost; approve or reject; and if approved, **re-baseline** so future variance is measured against the new plan --- not the old one you can no longer hit. **Configuration management** keeps the product definition (drawings, specs, software versions) in step with the approved baseline. ## Status reporting On a real project the reporting instruments are the periodic **status report** and the **dashboard**: they roll up progress, cost, schedule, risks, and issues on a fixed cadence. Good reporting is **honest** (report the red while it is still fixable), **consistent** (same metrics every period so trends are visible), and **actionable** (every variance has an owner and a next step). A dashboard that only ever shows green is not a control system --- it is a comfort blanket. ## Key Takeaways - **Control** is a closed loop: **measure → compare to baseline → analyze variance → act**, every reporting period. - Track **PV** (work scheduled), **EV** (work done), **AC** (money spent), all in budget dollars, against **BAC**. - $SV = EV - PV$, $CV = EV - AC$, $SPI = EV/PV$, $CPI = EV/AC$. Below 1 / negative = behind / over. - Forecast with **EAC** ($BAC/CPI$ is the common honest form), **ETC** $= EAC - AC$, **VAC** $= BAC - EAC$, **TCPI** $= (BAC-EV)/(BAC-AC)$. - **Spend is not progress.** Beware the **watermelon** report; watch **leading** indicators, not just SPI/CPI. - Keep the **baseline meaningful** through integrated change control and configuration management. - Report **honestly, consistently, and actionably** --- every variance gets an owner. ## Case Study: Meridian R/C — Week 12 ::: {.callout-tip .case-study title="📁 CASE STUDY FILE — Week 12: One Good Number Doesn't Make a Good Week"} Day 50, and it's time to run the loop this chapter just walked you through --- measure, compare, analyze, act --- against real Trailblazer numbers instead of a textbook example. Sofia Reyes's weekly report lands with a summary line that looks encouraging at a glance: spend is roughly tracking the plan. You know better than to stop at a glance. | Metric | Value | |---|---| | BAC (Budget At Completion) | \$761,300 | | PV (Planned Value, day 50) | \$560,000 | | EV (Earned Value, day 50) | \$520,000 | | AC (Actual Cost, day 50) | \$545,000 | You run the four core numbers yourself before the steering call. CV = EV − AC = \$520,000 − \$545,000 = **−\$25,000** --- over budget. SV = EV − PV = \$520,000 − \$560,000 = **−\$40,000** --- behind schedule. CPI = EV/AC = 520/545 ≈ **0.95**. SPI = EV/PV = 520/560 ≈ **0.93**. Running BAC/CPI forward gives an EAC of roughly **\$798,000** --- a forecast, not a certainty, but not a comfortable one either. The schedule slip traces to one place: activity H, toy-safety certification, which has sat on the critical path with zero float since the CPM network was first built back in Week 6. The certification lab pushed back its review date, and because H has no float, every day it slips is a day the whole 67-day project finish slips with it. The cost story is the sharper lesson. Two weeks ago, you talked MCS down from \$145,000 to **\$136,000** for the motor-and-controller package --- a genuine \$9,000 win, hard-negotiated, real money, and the whole point of using the competing Paragon quote as leverage. So why is AC still running \$25,000 ahead of EV? Because elsewhere on the project, packaging samples had to move by expedited freight to protect the schedule, and that bill quietly ate the MCS saving and then some. A favourable variance on one activity, read on its own, told the team nothing reliable about the project's overall health --- exactly the trap this chapter's "watermelon" warning describes: green on the outside, red once you look underneath. There is a sliver of good news buried in the bad. At roughly \$798,000, the EAC still sits just under Daniel Cho's \$800,000 charter ceiling from Week 3 --- a thin margin, but a margin, assuming nothing else slips before Week 13's closeout. ::: ## Practice Problems
Problem 1: Full EVM snapshot BAC = \$400 000. At the status date: PV = \$180 000, EV = \$150 000, AC = \$165 000. Compute SV, CV, SPI, CPI, EAC (BAC/CPI), ETC, VAC, TCPI, and state the project's condition in one sentence.
Solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} BAC <- 400000; PV <- 180000; EV <- 150000; AC <- 165000 SV <- EV - PV; CV <- EV - AC; SPI <- EV / PV; CPI <- EV / AC EAC <- BAC / CPI; ETC <- EAC - AC; VAC <- BAC - EAC TCPI <- (BAC - EV) / (BAC - AC) cat(sprintf("SV=$%s CV=$%s SPI=%.3f CPI=%.3f\n", format(SV, big.mark=" "), format(CV, big.mark=" "), SPI, CPI)) cat(sprintf("EAC=$%s ETC=$%s VAC=$%s TCPI=%.3f\n", format(round(EAC), big.mark=" "), format(round(ETC), big.mark=" "), format(round(VAC), big.mark=" "), TCPI)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` SV=$-30 000 CV=$-15 000 SPI=0.833 CPI=0.909 EAC=$440 000 ETC=$275 000 VAC=$-40 000 TCPI=1.064 ``` ::: ::: Behind schedule (SPI 0.83) and over cost (CPI 0.91); projected to finish about \$40 000 over budget, and the remaining work must run at TCPI ≈ 1.06 to still hit BAC.
Problem 2: On budget but in trouble A project reports PV = \$500 000, EV = \$400 000, AC = \$400 000. The sponsor sees "spend exactly matches earned value --- CPI = 1.0 --- we're fine." Are they?
Answer Cost efficiency is fine (CPI = 1.0), but **SPI = EV/PV = 0.80** --- the project has completed only 80 % of the work it should have by now. It is **20 % behind schedule** and will either finish late or need to spend more (overtime, added staff) to catch up, which will then push CPI below 1. This is the classic watermelon: the cost view is green, the schedule view is red.
Problem 3 (discussion): re-baseline or not? At week 8 the RC-vehicle project is forecast (EAC) at \$700 000 against a \$620 000 BAC, mostly because the retailer added a second body colourway (an approved scope change) and the new line's learning curve ran longer than planned. Should you re-baseline?
Discussion points Split the two causes. The **approved scope change** is a legitimate reason to re-baseline --- the extra colourway was authorised, so the budget and schedule should be formally updated and future variance measured against the new plan. The **learning-curve overrun** is *performance* against the plan, not a change to the plan --- that stays as variance you must recover or explain. Re-baselining to bury performance problems ("we'll just move the goalposts") destroys the value of the control system; re-baselining for authorised changes keeps it honest.
